newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's flood expenses seen keeping markets wary.
newsitem.headline: Poland's flood expenses seen keeping markets wary.

text.p: Poland's government, already working on gathering resources to clean up maor flood damage, is now also faced with having to contend with financial markets to keep them from wreaking more havoc on the country.

The government asked parliament on Wednesday to rush through laws making funds flow easier to flood-ravaged areas after last week's torrential downpour. But it will have to convince markets the special measures will not hurt Poland's economic stability.

Finance Minister Marek Belka reassured parliament the requested measures, which include seeking changes to the 1997 budget to allow the government to borrow up to 2.5 billion zlotys ($710.9 million) from the central bank for flood relief and asking for an increase in foreign borrowing limits to allow a $300 million World Bank soft loan, would not pump extra cash into the economy.

"The credit we asked from the NBP (National Bank of Poland) does not mean an increase in the total expenditures of the state. It only guarantees that we will not be in danger of losing liquidity," Belka said.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) Warsaw representative praised the government for trying to tread a thin line between efforts to ensure sufficient funds are available to deal with the damage and maintaining financial stability.
But analysts remained wary, saying only estimates of the total costs and information on how much and in what way the government would borrow could soothe worries about the disaster's economic impact.
Foreign exchange traders said uncertainty over budget performance this year and possible central bank actions added to already existing concerns over Poland's trade deficit and hit the zloty hard.
The zloty lost a record five percent on Tuesday. And though it recovered about 2.5 percent with central bank help on Wednesday, the market remained jittery.
Warsaw shares fell 5.2 percent in the three sessions to Tuesday before rebounding one percent on Wednesday.

The central bank volunteered a one billion zloty emergency loan on Tuesday at market rates and promised to fully offset its monetary impact by drawing money from the market by accepting deposits from the public.

But analysts said it was not clear the government would accept the offer. "Much will depend on whether the actual borrowing will be closer to the NBP's one billion or nearer the 2.5 billion ceiling because the latter would definitely have inflationary effects," a senior economist at a foreign institution said.
The government aims to cut year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December and to 9.5 percent at 1998-end from 15.3 percent last month.
Analysts were disappointed the government abandoned the idea of a special flood tax.

"The decision not to finance flood reconstruction by a tax could create a certain inflationary impulse," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, chief analyst at government's Centre for Strategic Studies. "The 13-percent (inflation) target for this year is still realistic, but we will not get any lower. Inflationary impulses from higher government borrowing will spill over to next year, and the 9.5-percent target is threatened."
The government stressed it would seek to finance the reconstruction mainly by shifting funds within the budget and that it has already lined up 650 million zlotys in this way.

But several analysts were sceptical the 1997 budget deficit target of 2.8 percent, already under pressure from lower tax revenues and high deficit financing costs, would withstand pressure from possible revenue loss and higher spending needs.
Analysts said Poland's 5.5-percent growth targets for this and next year would be least affected because losses in farming and industrial output could be offset by a building boom.
But they noted that reconstruction efforts would boost demand for imports, which would probably push the trade deficit this year beyond the earlier-predicted $12 billion.
